introduction-the-invisible-hand-shaping-.core: Conway's Law: organisations design systems that mirror their communication structures. Team boundaries become module, service and API boundaries, whether you intend them to or not.

first_principles.problem: Software looks like the org chart: four teams produce a four-stage pipeline, even when one service would be better.
truths: People coordinate most easily within teams.
Boundaries form where communication is hardest.
derivation: Use the **Inverse Conway Maneuver**: design the teams for the architecture you want.
Manage **cognitive load** and **team APIs**; keep teams **long-lived**.

analogy.title: A building shaped by its construction crews
analogy.story: If plumbing, electrical and framing crews never talk, the house ends up with pipes and wires fighting for the same walls.
analogy.breaks: Conway's Law describes a strong tendency, not an absolute rule. Strong architecture leadership can resist it partially.

example.title: Three teams, three tiers
flow: Architecture = 3 rigid tiers with slow handoffs

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The org chart shaped the architecture.

example.outcome: you can see how org design drives architecture.

check.a: Organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structures.

the-problem-when-structure-fights-strate.core: If the target architecture (say, independent microservices) conflicts with the team structure (say, functional silos), the org structure wins: services become entangled and coordination costs balloon.

first_principles.problem: A company 'adopts microservices' but keeps functional teams, and ends up with a distributed monolith where every change needs four teams.
truths: Architecture intent loses to daily coordination needs.
derivation: **Map** teams to the intended service boundaries.

analogy.title: A sports team with positions that don't match the tactics
analogy.story: You plan fast wing play, but nobody's assigned to the wings.
analogy.breaks: Reorgs are costly and disruptive, so only realign where the friction is real.

example.title: Measuring the mismatch
flow: Add a field to user profile
Needs UI, API, DB, mobile teams

check.q: What's a 'distributed monolith' in Conway's Law terms?
check.a: Separately deployed services that remain tightly coupled because the teams behind them still coordinate as one.

the-solution-the-inverse-conway-maneuver.core: Since structure shapes architecture, design the team structure first to match the architecture you want: stream-aligned teams owning specific domains or services, so the communication paths produce the desired boundaries.

first_principles.problem: Teams try to impose architecture through diagrams alone, but the communication structure keeps undoing it.
truths: Conway's force can be used deliberately.
Teams own what they can change independently.
derivation: Form **teams per domain** with end-to-end ownership.

analogy.title: Laying paths before people walk
analogy.story: Shape where people walk by designing the paths (team structure), and the traffic patterns (architecture) follow.
analogy.breaks: A badly chosen domain split will be faithfully mirrored too, so get the domains right.

example.title: Reorganising for domains
example.outcome: architecture that's reinforced by the organisation.

check.q: What is the Inverse Conway Maneuver?
check.a: Deliberately structuring teams to match the desired architecture so the system evolves toward it.

cognitive-load-the-teams-cpu-limit.core: Teams have a finite capacity to understand and own things. Intrinsic (inherent complexity), extraneous (tooling friction) and germane (domain learning) load all compete. Overloaded teams slow down and make mistakes, so size ownership to capacity.

first_principles.problem: One team owns 14 services, three languages and the infrastructure, so everything is slow and quality suffers.
derivation: Give each team **ownership it can fully understand**.
**Reduce extraneous load** through platforms and paved roads.
**Split** domains when the load exceeds capacity.

analogy.title: A computer's CPU limit
analogy.story: Run too many programs and everything slows; close the background apps (extraneous load) first.
analogy.breaks: Load isn't only the number of services. One complex service can exceed the capacity of a team.

example.title: An overloaded team
flow: Two domains split to a new team

check.q: Which type of cognitive load should platforms aim to reduce?
check.a: Extraneous load, the friction of tools, infrastructure and processes unrelated to the team's domain.

the-team-api-communication-as-code.core: A team API defines how other teams interact with it: its owned services and APIs, documentation, communication channels, request process, working hours and SLAs. Explicit interfaces between teams reduce ad-hoc coordination, just like software APIs.

first_principles.problem: Other teams don't know how to ask for help or changes, so they DM random engineers and constantly interrupt them.
truths: Documentation scales better than tribal knowledge.
derivation: Describe **how to engage** (channels, ticket forms, office hours).

analogy.title: A shop's opening hours and service desk
analogy.story: Customers know when to come, where to go and what service to expect, without wandering into the stockroom.
analogy.breaks: Too much process makes teams feel bureaucratic, so keep the API lightweight.

code.text:
# Team Payments — Team API
**We own:** payments-api, ledger, refunds worker
**Ask us:** #payments-help (triaged daily), Jira PAY intake form
**Office hours:** Tue/Thu 14:00 UTC
**SLA:** P1 bugs 4h, feature requests reviewed weekly
**Roadmap:** link

check.q: What's the purpose of a team API?
check.a: To define clearly how other teams interact with a team, reducing ad-hoc interruptions and coordination cost.

long-lived-teams-vs-project-teams.core: Project teams that disband after delivery leave orphaned software whose architecture decays. Long-lived, stable teams own products over time, accumulating domain knowledge and keeping the system coherent.

first_principles.problem: Projects end, the team scatters, and the service becomes an unowned liability nobody understands.
truths: Stable teams build trust and velocity.
derivation: Bring **work to stable teams** rather than forming teams per project.

analogy.title: A garden needs a permanent gardener
analogy.story: Planting crews that leave after planting mean the garden is overgrown within a season.
analogy.breaks: Some exploratory work suits temporary teams, but production systems need permanent owners.

example.title: The orphaned service
flow: Fix: assign to Payments team permanently
example.outcome: systems that stay coherent over time.

check.q: Why do disbanded project teams cause architectural decay?
check.a: Without ongoing owners, knowledge is lost and changes become ad hoc, eroding the system's coherence.
